section.heading: 2.6. The Derivative
An Intuitive Example
section.paragraph: We mentioned in Section 2.4 that the problem of finding the rate of change of one quantity with respect to another is mathematically equivalent to the problem of finding the slope of the tangent line to a curve at a given point on the curve. Before going on to establish this relationship, let’s show its plausibility by looking at it from an intuitive point of view.
Consider the motion of the maglev discussed in Section 2.4. Recall that the position of the maglev at any time $$t$$ is given by
where $$s$$ is measured in feet and $$t$$ in seconds. The graph of the function $$f$$ is sketched in Figure 48.

image.alt: Details A curve s = f(t) is graphed on a coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t ranges from around 0 to about 4 seconds. The vertical axis s ranges from below 0 to over 60 feet. The curve begins at the origin, rises upward to the right, increasingly bulging away from the y axis, as it rises upward to the right into the first quadrant till around (4.2, 80).

figure.caption: Graph showing the position $$s$$ of a maglev at time $$t$$

section.paragraph: Observe that the graph of $$f$$ rises slowly at first but more rapidly as $$t$$ increases, reflecting the fact that the speed of the maglev is increasing with time. This observation suggests a relationship between the speed of the maglev at any time $$t$$ and the steepness of the curve at the point corresponding to this value of $$t$$ . Thus, it would appear that we can solve the problem of finding the speed of the maglev at any time if we can find a way to measure the steepness of the curve at any point on the curve.

To discover a yardstick that will measure the steepness of a curve, consider the graph of a function $$f$$ such as the one shown in Figure 49a. Think of the curve as representing a stretch of roller coaster track (Figure 49b). When the car is at the point $$P$$ on the curve, a passenger sitting erect in the car and looking straight ahead will have a line of sight that is parallel to the line $$T$$ , the tangent to the curve at $$P$$ .

image.alt: Details Two images a and b Image a: A curve y = f(x) and its tangent T are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins near the bottom right of the first quadrant, rises upward to the right, bulging away from the x axis, reaches a high point and then descends to the right, reaches a low point and then rises upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis. A line is drawn entirely above the curve with a positive slope. It begins near the y axis, rises upward to the right and touches the curve at a point labeled P(x, f(x)) when it first rises upward to the right. Image b: The exact same curve and the tangent are drawn in Image b with only the curve and the tangent labeled y = f(x) and T respectively. Below the curve, equidistant vertical, horizontal and slanted lines running upward to the right and downward to the left are drawn below the curve forming a grid. Above the tangent, the silhouettes of the busts of three people are drawn. A line segment is drawn parallel to the tangent labeled line of sight.

section.paragraph: As Figure 49a suggests, the steepness of the curve—that is, the rate at which $$y$$ is increasing or decreasing with respect to $$x$$ —is given by the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ . But for now we will show how this relationship can be used to estimate the rate of change of a function from its graph.

note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: From the figure, we see that the slope of the tangent line $$T_{1}$$ to the graph of $$y = N(t)$$ at $$P_{1}(10,44.7)$$ is approximately $$0.5$$ . This tells us that the quantity $$y$$ is increasing at the rate of $$\frac{1}{2}$$ unit per unit increase in $$t$$ , when $$t = 10$$ . In other words, at the beginning of the year 2000, the number of Social Security beneficiaries was increasing at the rate of approximately $$0.5$$ millon, or $$500,000$$ , per year.

The slope of the tangent line $$T_{2}$$ at $$P_{2}(35,71.9)$$ is approximately $$1.15$$ . This tells us that at the beginning of 2025 the number of Social Security beneficiaries will be growing at the rate of approximately $$1.15$$ million, or $$1,150,000$$ , per year.

section.heading: Slope of a Tangent Line
section.paragraph: In Example 1, we answered the questions raised by drawing the graph of the function $$N$$ and estimating the position of the tangent lines. Ideally, however, we would like to solve a problem analytically whenever possible. To do this, we need a precise definition of the slope of a tangent line to a curve.

To define the tangent line to a curve $$C$$ at a point $$P$$ on the curve, fix $$P$$ and let $$Q$$ be any point on $$C$$ distinct from $$P$$ (Figure 51). The straight line passing through $$P$$ and $$Q$$ is called a secant line .

image.alt: Details A curve C is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins near the y axis a short distance above the x axis, descends to the right, bulging down, reaches a low point labeled P(x, f(x)),continues to rise upward to the right into the first quadrant, bulging towards the x axis. A point labeled Q is located near the top right of the curve. Three unlabelled points are marked on the curve between P and Q. Four lines rising upward to the right are drawn passing through P and each of the other 4 points. All four lines are together labeled Secant lines. One line is drawn entirely below the curve. It starts from the bottom left, touches the curve at P(x, f(x)) and then gradually rises upward to the right.

figure.caption: As $$Q$$ approaches $$P$$ along the curve $$C$$ , the secant lines approach the tangent line $$T$$ .

section.paragraph: Now, as the point $$Q$$ is allowed to move toward $$P$$ along the curve, the secant line through $$P$$ and $$Q$$ rotates about the fixed point $$P$$ and approaches a fixed line through $$P$$ . This fixed line, which is the limiting position of the secant lines through $$P$$ and $$Q$$ as $$Q$$ approaches $$P$$ , is the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$P$$ .

We can describe the process more precisely as follows. Suppose the curve $$C$$ is the graph of a function $$f$$ defined by $$y = f(x)$$ . Then the point $$P$$ is described by $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and the point $$Q$$ by $$Q\left( x + h,f(x + h) \right)$$ , where $$h$$ is some appropriate nonzero number (Figure 52a). Observe that we can make $$Q$$ approach $$P$$ along the curve $$C$$ by letting $$h$$ approach zero (Figure 52b).

image.alt: Details The image has two graphs. On the left, a curve C defined by y = f(x) and a line graphed are in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins near the y axis a short distance above the x axis, descends to the right, bulging downward and reaches a low point labeled P(x, f(x)), rises upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis, passes through another point labeled Q((x + h), f(x + h)) and continues into the first quadrant. From the point P(x, f(x)), a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis, meeting it at the mark labeled x. From the point Q ((x + h), f(x + h)), a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis, meeting it at the mark labeled x + h. A line begins near the x axis, rises upward to the right and cuts the curve at two points: P(x, f(x)), Q ((x + h), f(x + h)). The second curve begins near the y axis a short distance above the x axis, descends to the right, bulging downward and reaches a low point labeled P(x, f(x)), rises upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis, and continues into the first quadrant. The points P, situated near the bottom left of the curve, and Q, located near the top right of the curve, are labeled. Three unlabelled points are marked on the curve between P and Q. The horizontal distance between P and each of the other points is labeled h.

section.paragraph: Next, using the formula for the slope of a line, we can write the slope of the secant line passing through $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and $$Q\left( x + h,f(x + h) \right)$$ as
$$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{(x + h) - x} = \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

As we observed earlier, $$Q$$ approaches $$P$$ , and therefore the secant line through $$P$$ and $$Q$$ approaches the tangent line $$T$$ as $$h$$ approaches zero. Consequently, we might expect that the slope of the secant line would approach the slope of the tangent line $$T$$ as $$h$$ approaches zero. This leads to the following definition.

note.title: Slope of a Tangent Line
note.heading: Slope of a Tangent Line
note.paragraph: The slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ is given by
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$
if it exists.

section.heading: Rates of Change
section.paragraph: We now show that the problem of finding the slope of the tangent line to the graph of a function $$f$$ at the point $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ is mathematically equivalent to the problem of finding the rate of change of $$f$$ at $$x$$ . To see this, suppose we are given a function $$f$$ that describes the relationship between the two quantities $$x$$ and $$y$$ —that is, $$y = f(x)$$ . The number $$f(x + h) - f(x)$$ measures the change in $$y$$ that corresponds to a change $$h$$ in $$x$$ (Figure 53).

image.alt: Details A curve y = f(x) is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins near the y axis, descends to the right bulging down, reaches a low point and continues to rise upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis. From a mark labeled f(x) on the y axis, a line parallel to the x axis runs to the right cutting the curve at two points, the one on the right is labeled P(x, f(x)). From this point a perpendicular is drawn to the x axis meeting it at a point labeled x. From a mark labeled f(x + h) on the y axis, above the mark f(x), another horizontal line runs to the right, parallel to the x axis, and meets the curve at a point marked Q(x + h, f(x + h)). From this point a perpendicular is drawn to the x axis meeting it at a mark labeled x + h. The distance between the two perpendiculars to the x axis reaching the x axis at x and x + h, is labeled h. The distance between the two lines parallel to the x axis at f(x) and f(x + h) is labeled f(x + h) – f(x).

figure.caption: $$f(x + h) - f(x)$$ is the change in $$y$$ that corresponds to a change $$h$$ in $$x$$ .

section.paragraph: Then, the difference quotient
$$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

measures the average rate of change of $$\mathbf{y}$$ with respect to $$\mathbf{x}$$ over the interval $$\lbrack x,x + h\rbrack$$ . For example, if $$y$$ measures the position of a car at time $$x$$ , then quotient (7) gives the average velocity of the car over the time interval $$\lbrack x,x + h\rbrack$$ .

Observe that the difference quotient (7) is the same as (5). We conclude that the difference quotient (7) also measures the slope of the secant line that passes through the two points $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and $$Q\left( x + h,f(x + h) \right)$$ lying on the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ . Next, by taking the limit of the difference quotient (7) as $$h$$ goes to zero—that is, by evaluating
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

we obtain the rate of change of $$\mathbf{f}$$ at $$\mathbf{x}$$ . For example, if $$y$$ measures the position of a car at time $$x$$ , then the limit (8) gives the velocity of the car at time $$x$$ . For emphasis, the rate of change of a function $$f$$ at $$x$$ is often called the instantaneous rate of change of $$\mathbf{f}$$ at $$\mathbf{x}$$ . This distinguishes it from the average rate of change of $$f$$ , which is computed over an interval $$\lbrack x,x + h\rbrack$$ rather than at a number $$x$$ .

Observe that the limit (8) is the same as (6). Therefore, the limit of the difference quotient also measures the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ at the point $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ . The following summarizes this discussion.

note.source_type: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change
note.title: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change
note.heading: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change
note.paragraph: The average rate of change of $$f$$ over the interval $$\lbrack x,x + h\rbrack$$ or slope of the secant line to the graph of $$f$$ through the points $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and $$\left( x + h,f(x + h) \right)$$ is
$$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$
The instantaneous rate of change of $$f$$ at $$x$$ or slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ is
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow\infty}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

note.heading: Explore and Discuss

section.heading: The Derivative
section.paragraph: The limit $$(6)$$ or $$(10)$$ , which measures both the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ at the point $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and the (instantaneous) rate of change of $$f$$ at $$x$$ , is given a special name: the derivative of $$\mathbf{f}$$ at $$\mathbf{x}$$ .

note.title: Derivative of a Function
note.heading: Derivative of a Function
note.paragraph: The derivative of a function $$f$$ with respect to $$x$$ is the function $$f^{\prime}$$ (read “ $$f$$ prime”),
$$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$
The domain of $$f^{\prime}$$ is the set of all $$x$$ for which the limit exists.

section.paragraph: Thus, the derivative of a function $$f$$ is a function $$f^{\prime}$$ that gives the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at any point $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ and also the rate of change of $$f$$ at $$x$$ (Figure 54).

image.alt: Details A curve y = f(x) and a line T are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins in the second quadrant at a distance above the negative x axis, rises upward to the right, cuts the y axis, rises upward to the right, bulging away from the x axis, reaches a peak and then descends to the right, reaches a low point and then rises upward, passing through a labeled point P(x, f(x)) now bulging down towards the x axis. The line begins near the x axis, rises upward to the right with a positive slope and touches the curve near its second inflection point as it rises to the right. The point where the tangent touches the curve is labeled P(x, f(x)). A vertical line segment from the mark x rises upward from the x axis, parallel to the y axis and meets the curve and the line at P(x, f(x)). Another line segment starts from P, runs horizontally to the right parallel to the x axis accompanied by the text 1. From the end of this line segment, another line segment runs vertically upward accompanied by the text f prime (x).

figure.caption: The slope of the tangent line at $$P\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ is $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ ; $$f$$ changes at the rate of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ units per unit change in $$x$$ at $$x$$ .

section.paragraph: Other notations for the derivative of $$f$$ include the following:
$$\begin{array}{ll} {D_{x}f(x)} & { {{Read}{}_{}^{}{sub}x{of}f{of}x^{"}}} \\ \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} & { {{Read}{}_{}^{}ydx^{"}}} \\ y^{\prime} & { {{Read}{}_{}^{}{prime}^{"}}} \end{array}$$
The last two are used when the rule for $$f$$ is written in the form $$y = f(x)$$ .
The calculation of the derivative of $$f$$ is facilitated by using the following four-step process.

note.source_type: Four-Step Process for Finding f ′ ( x )
note.title: Four-Step Process for Finding f ′ ( x )
note.heading: Four-Step Process for Finding f ′ ( x )

list.item: Compute $$f(x + h)$$ .
Form the difference $$f(x + h) - f(x)$$ .
Form the quotient $$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$ .
Compute the limit $$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f(x) = 3x + 5$$ at any point $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The slope of the tangent line at any point on the graph of $$f$$ is given by the derivative of $$f$$ at $$x$$ . To find the derivative, we use the four-step process:
example.heading: Step 1
Step 2
Step 3
Step 4
example.paragraph: We expect this result, since the tangent line to any point on a straight line must coincide with the line itself and therefore must have the same slope as the line. In this case, the graph of $$f$$ is a straight line with slope 3.

list.item: Find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .
Compute $$f^{\prime}(2)$$ and interpret your result.

To find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , we use the four-step process: Step 1 $$f(x + h) = (x + h)^{2} = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2}$$ Step 2 $$f(x + h) - f(x) = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - x^{2} = 2xh + h^{2} = h(2x + h)$$ Step 3 $$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = \frac{h(2x + h)}{h} = 2x + h$$ Step 4 $$f^{\prime}{(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f{(x)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}(2x + h) = 2x$$

$$f^{\prime}(2) = 2(2) = 4$$ . This result tells us that the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$(2,4)$$ is $$4$$ . It also tells us that the function $$f$$ is changing at the rate of $$4$$ units per unit change in $$x$$ at $$x = 2$$ . The graph of $$f$$ and the tangent line at $$(2,4)$$ are shown in Figure 55.

list.item: Consider the function $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ of Example 3. Suppose we want to compute $$f^{\prime}(2)$$ , using Equation (11). Thus, $$f^{\prime}(2) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {2 + h} \right) - f(2)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left( {2 + h} \right)^{2} - 2^{2}}{h}$$ Use a graphing utility to plot the graph of $$g(x) = \frac{\left( {2 + x} \right)^{2} - 4}{x}$$ in the viewing window $$\lbrack - 3,3\rbrack \times \lbrack - 2,6\rbrack$$ .

Explain why the limit found in part 2 is $$f^{\prime}(2)$$ .
Find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .
Find the point on the graph of $$f$$ where the tangent line to the curve is horizontal.
Sketch the graph of $$f$$ and the tangent line to the curve at the point found in part (b).
What is the rate of change of $$f$$ at this point?

To find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , we use the four-step process: Step 1 $$f\left( {x + h} \right) = \left( {x + h} \right)^{2} - 4\left( {x + h} \right) = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 4x - 4h$$ Step 2 $$\begin{array}{l} {f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x) = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 4x - 4h - {({x^{2} - 4x})}} \\ {\phantom{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)} = 2\mathit{xh} + h^{2} - 4h = h\left( {2x + h - 4} \right)} \end{array}$$ Step 3 $$\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \frac{h{({2x + h - 4})}}{h} = 2x + h - 4$$ Step 4 $$f^{\prime}{(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{({2x + h - 4})} = 2x - 4$$

At a point on the graph of $$f$$ where the tangent line to the curve is horizontal and hence has slope zero, the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of $$f$$ is zero. Accordingly, to find such point(s), we set $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ , which gives $$2x - 4 = 0$$ or $$x = 2$$ . The corresponding value of $$y$$ is given by $$y = f(2) = - 4$$ , and the required point is $$(2, - 4)$$ .

The graph of $$f$$ and the tangent line are shown in Figure 56. Using the definition given in Part 3, formulate a four-step process for finding $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ similar to that given in Four-Step Process for Finding f(x), and use it to find the derivative of $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ . Compare your answer with that obtained in Example 3.

note.source_type: Applied Example 6. Velocity of a Car
note.title: Applied Example 6. Velocity of a Car
note.heading: Applied Example 6. Velocity of a Car
note.paragraph: Suppose the distance (in feet) covered by a car moving along a straight road $$t$$ seconds after starting from rest is given by the function $$f(t) = 2t^{2}\left( {0 \leq t \leq 30} \right)$$ .

list.item: Calculate the average velocity of the car over the time intervals $$\lbrack 22,23\rbrack$$ , $$\lbrack 22,22.1\rbrack$$ , and $$\lbrack 22,22.01\rbrack$$ .
Calculate the (instantaneous) velocity of the car when $$t = 22$$ .
Compare the results obtained in part (a) with that obtained in part (b).

note.heading: Solution

list.item: We first compute the average velocity (average rate of change of $$f$$ ) over the interval $$\lbrack t,t + h\rbrack$$ using Formula (9). We find $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{f\left( {t + h} \right) - f(t)}{h} = \frac{2\left( {t + h} \right)^{2} - 2t^{2}}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f\left( {t + h} \right) - f(t)}{h}} = \frac{2t^{2} + 4th + 2h^{2} - 2t^{2}}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f\left( {t + h} \right) - f(t)}{h}} = 4t + 2h} \end{array}$$ Next, using $$t = 22$$ and $$h = 1$$ , we find that the average velocity of the car over the time interval $$\lbrack 22,23\rbrack$$ is $$4(22) + 2(1) = 90$$ or $$90{ft}/\sec$$ . Similarly, using $$t = 22$$ , $$h = 0.1$$ , and $$h = 0.01$$ , we find that its average velocities over the time intervals $$\lbrack 22,22.1\rbrack$$ and $$\lbrack 22,22.01\rbrack$$ are $$88.2$$ and $$88.02{ft}/\sec$$ , respectively.

Using the limit $$(10)$$ , we see that the instantaneous velocity of the car at any time $$t$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {t + h} \right) - f(t)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left( {4t + 2h} \right) { \text{Use the results from part} (a).}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {t + h} \right) - f(t)}{h}} = 4t} \end{array}$$ In particular, the velocity of the car $$22$$ seconds from rest $$(t = 22)$$ is given by $$\upsilon = 4(22)$$ or $$88{ft}/\sec$$ .

The computations in part (a) show that, as the time intervals over which the average velocity of the car are computed become smaller and smaller, the average velocities over these intervals do approach $$88{ft}/\sec$$ , the instantaneous velocity of the car at $$t = 22$$ .

list.item: Find the average rate of change in the unit price of a tire if the quantity demanded is between $$5000$$ and $$6000$$ tires, between $$5000$$ and $$5100$$ tires, and between $$5000$$ and $$5010$$ tires.
What is the instantaneous rate of change of the unit price when the quantity demanded is $$5000$$ units?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: The average rate of change of the unit price of a tire if the quantity demanded (in thousands) is between $$x$$ and $$x + h$$ is $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \frac{\lbrack 144 - {({x + h})}^{2}\rbrack - ({144 - x^{2}})}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h}} = \frac{144 - x^{2} - 2xh - h^{2} - 144 + x^{2}}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h}} = - 2x - h} \end{array}$$ To find the average rate of change of the unit price of a tire when the quantity demanded is between $$5000$$ and $$6000$$ tires (that is, over the interval $$\lbrack 5,6\rbrack$$ ), we take $$x = 5$$ and $$h = 1$$ , obtaining $$- 2(5) - 1 = - 11$$ or $$- \$ 11$$ per $$1000$$ tires. (Remember, $$x$$ is measured in units of a thousand.) Similarly, taking $$h = 0.1$$ and $$h = 0.01$$ with $$x = 5$$ , we find that the average rates of change of the unit price when the quantities demanded are between $$5000$$ and $$5100$$ and between $$5000$$ and $$5010$$ are $$- \$ 10.10$$ and $$- \$ 10.01$$ per $$1000$$ tires, respectively.

The instantaneous rate of change of the unit price of a tire when the quantity demanded is $$x$$ units is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left( {- 2x - h} \right) { \text{Use the results from part} (a).}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h}} = - 2x} \end{array}$$ In particular, the instantaneous rate of change of the unit price per tire when the quantity demanded is $$5000$$ is given by $$- 2(5)$$ , or $$- \$ 10$$ per $$1000$$ tires.

section.heading: Differentiability and Continuity
section.paragraph: In practical applications, one encounters continuous functions that fail to be differentiable —that is, do not have a derivative—at certain values in the domain of the function $$f$$ . It can be shown that a continuous function $$f$$ fails to be differentiable at $$x = a$$ when the graph of $$f$$ makes an abrupt change of direction at $$\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ . We call such a point a “corner.” A function also fails to be differentiable at a point where the tangent line is vertical, since the slope of a vertical line is undefined. These cases are illustrated in Figure 59.

image.alt: Details There are two graphs a and b. In image a, a curve is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. It begins in the second quadrant close to the negative x axis in the bottom left, rises upward to the right, bulging slightly upward intersecting the y axis at an unmarked point till it reaches a peak at a point marked (a, f(a)). From here, the curve descends downward to the right, bulging slightly downward. From the peak point, a perpendicular is drawn to the x axis meeting it at a labeled point a. In image b, a curve is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. From the x axis, at a mark labeled a, a line extends vertically upward, parallel to the y axis, cutting the curve at (a, f(a)). The curve begins near the x axis in the first quadrant a little away from the origin, rises upward to the right, bulging towards the x axis, briefly straightens out as it meets the line x = a, at the point labeled (a, f(a)), after which it rises upward to the right, bulging away from the x axis.

The line begins at the origin, rises upward to the right till the labeled point (8, 80). From here, the line deviates to the left, rising up again linearly but with a steeper slope.

section.paragraph: We close this section by mentioning the connection between the continuity and the differentiability of a function at a given value $$x = a$$ in the domain of $$f$$ . By reexamining the function of Example 8, it becomes clear that $$f$$ is continuous everywhere and, in particular, when $$x = 8$$ . This shows that in general the continuity of a function at $$x = a$$ does not necessarily imply the differentiability of the function at that number. The converse, however, is true: If a function $$f$$ is differentiable at $$x = a$$ , then it is continuous there.

note.paragraph: If a function is differentiable at $$x = a$$ , then it is continuous at $$x = a$$ .

example.paragraph: Figure 61 depicts a portion of the graph of a function. Explain why the function fails to be differentiable at each of the numbers $$x = a,b,c,d,e,f$$ , and $$g$$ .

image.alt: Details A function is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. Line segments from the x axis rise upward to meet the curve at the labeled points a, b, c, d, e, f, and g. The intervals between the line segments are not equal. The curve begins from the third quadrant, rises upward to the right, bulging away from the x axis, cuts the x axis, enters into the second quadrant, cuts the y axis, continues upward to the right till it reaches the line segment from x = a where it ends with an open circle. The next part of the curve begins with a closed circle directly above the open circle on the line x = a, descends downward to the right, bulging downward, towards the x axis, till it meets the line at x = b with an open circle where it inflects and then continues to rise steeply upward to the right running almost parallel to the line at x = c. From the line x = c a little above the inflection point of the previous segment of the curve, a line segment begins with a closed circle, runs horizontally to the right parallel to the x axis to meet the line at x = d. From x = d, a line segment rises up to the right till it meets the vertical line at x = e. From this point, the line slopes downward to the left till it reaches the line at x = f. From this point, a curve rises upward to the right, bulging away from the x axis at first, reaches a peak and then descends to the right, bulging down, reaches a low point and then steeply rises to meet the line at x = g. From x = g, the curve arches upward and almost levels out at the top right.

figure.caption: The graph of this function is not differentiable at the numbers $$a - g$$ .

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The function fails to be differentiable at $$x = a,b$$ , and $$c$$ because it is discontinuous at each of these numbers. The derivative of the function does not exist at $$x = d,e$$ , and $$f$$ because it has a kink at each point on the graph corresponding to these numbers. Finally, the function is not differentiable at $$x = g$$ because the tangent line is vertical at the corresponding point on the graph.
